questions.stem: A 74 year old man has a 4 month history of upper abdominal discomfort, early fullness after meals and 7 kg unintentional weight loss. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 50 years. He has conjunctival pallor and mild epigastric tenderness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Weight loss, dyspepsia and iron deficiency anaemia in an older smoker point to gastric adenocarcinoma, the most common gastric malignancy; GORD and peptic ulcer do not explain the weight loss.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Older smoker, dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss and microcytic anaemia: an upper GI malignancy until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastric adenocarcinoma.

elim: Causes pain radiating to the back and steatorrhoea, often with alcohol.
Causes diarrhoea and malabsorption, rarely presenting first at 74 with dyspepsia.
Can bleed, but 7 kg weight loss with early satiety in a 74 year old smoker suggests cancer.
Does not cause weight loss or iron deficiency anaemia; those are red flags.

steps.x: **D. Gastric adenocarcinoma.** Old + dyspepsia + weight loss + anaemia = gastric cancer until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 5 month history of epigastric pain, anorexia and 9 kg weight loss. On examination there is a firm epigastric mass and a hard, non-tender 1 cm nodule in the skin at her umbilicus. Her temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 88 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely name for the umbilical finding?
questions.e: A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical subcutaneous metastasis, a late sign of gastric cancer; Cullen's sign is bruising, not a nodule.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: hard, non-tender 1 cm nodule in the skin at her umbilicus
steps.x: A hard umbilical nodule in intra-abdominal malignancy is a subcutaneous metastasis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sister Mary Joseph nodule.

elim: Periumbilical bruising from retroperitoneal haemorrhage, e.g. pancreatitis.
Flank bruising in haemorrhagic pancreatitis.
Pain on inspiration during RUQ palpation in cholecystitis.
A palpable left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node.

steps.x: **D. Sister Mary Joseph nodule.** Umbilical metastasis = Sister Mary Joseph nodule.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has a 3 month history of indigestion, vomiting and 8 kg weight loss. On examination there is a hard, fixed 2 cm lymph node just above the medial end of his left clavicle. His abdomen is soft. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely name for this examination finding?
questions.e: A palpable Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) is Troisier's sign, from lymphatic spread of gastric cancer via the thoracic duct.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: indigestion, vomiting and 8 kg weight loss
steps.x: A palpable left supraclavicular node in a patient with an upper GI cancer picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Troisier's sign.

elim: A palpable painless gallbladder with jaundice in pancreatic cancer.
Inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation in cholecystitis.
RIF pain on LIF palpation in appendicitis.
An umbilical metastasis.

steps.x: **E. Troisier's sign.** Left supraclavicular node = Virchow's node = Troisier's sign.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has bilateral solid ovarian masses on pelvic ultrasound. She also has 4 months of epigastric pain, early satiety and 6 kg weight loss. OGD shows a thickened, rigid stomach wall without a discrete mass. Biopsies of the stomach and one ovary are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on histology of both biopsies?
questions.e: A Krukenberg tumour is bilateral ovarian metastasis of signet ring cell gastric adenocarcinoma; signet ring cells are the distinguishing histology of the diffuse subtype.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: early satiety and 6 kg weight loss
thickened, rigid stomach wall without a discrete mass
steps.x: Bilateral ovarian metastases from a diffuse gastric cancer: a Krukenberg tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Signet ring cells.

elim: Seen in serous ovarian and papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Found in Hodgkin lymphoma.
Describe a gastrointestinal stromal tumour.
Describe squamous cell carcinoma.

steps.x: **C. Signet ring cells.** Krukenberg tumour = signet ring cells from the stomach.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has ankle swelling, epigastric discomfort and vomiting. Serum albumin is 21 g/L with no proteinuria and normal liver tests. OGD shows giant, thickened rugal folds in the body of the stomach. Biopsy shows foveolar hyperplasia with loss of parietal cells, and gastric pH testing shows achlorhydria. There is no malignancy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Menetrier's disease is hypertrophy of the gastric mucosa with achlorhydria and protein loss, and is a risk factor for gastric cancer; Zollinger–Ellison causes acid excess.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Hypertrophic gastric mucosa, protein loss and achlorhydria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Menetrier's disease.

elim: Thins the mucosa rather than causing giant folds.
A lymphoid infiltrate on biopsy; it is malignant.
Causes a discrete ulcer, not giant folds with protein loss.
Thick folds but with acid hypersecretion and ulcers, not achlorhydria.

steps.x: **C. Menetrier's disease.** Giant rugae + achlorhydria + low albumin = Menetrier's disease.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has gastric adenocarcinoma diagnosed on OGD. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day, drinks 14 units of alcohol a week, takes omeprazole and has a family history of bowel cancer. Gastric biopsies show chronic active gastritis with curved Gram-negative rods.
questions.q: Which risk factor most strongly increased his risk of this cancer?
questions.e: H. pylori is an extremely strong risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma, raising risk about 6-fold; smoking, high alcohol intake, pernicious anaemia and chronic gastritis also contribute.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Curved Gram-negative rods on gastric biopsy are H. pylori.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Helicobacter pylori infection.

elim: A risk factor, but 14 units a week is modest and weaker than H. pylori.
Not a strong risk factor for sporadic gastric cancer.
Not an established cause; PPIs are often started for the symptoms.
A risk factor, but weaker than H. pylori.

steps.x: **C. Helicobacter pylori infection.** Strongest gastric cancer risk factor: H. pylori (about 6-fold).

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has known gastric adenocarcinoma and declined treatment 6 months ago. He now has worsening abdominal distension, anorexia and fatigue. He is cachectic. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Hepatomegaly with a smooth, tender edge
Palpable epigastric mass with shifting dullness
questions.e: Late findings of gastric cancer are an epigastric mass, Virchow's node and malignant ascites (shifting dullness).

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Untreated advanced gastric cancer with distension: an epigastric mass and ascites.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palpable epigastric mass with shifting dullness.

elim: More typical of right heart failure or hepatitis.
Courvoisier's sign of pancreatic cancer.
An abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Typical of an appendix mass or Crohn's disease.

steps.x: **B. Palpable epigastric mass with shifting dullness.** Late gastric cancer: epigastric mass, Virchow's node, ascites.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 3 months of early satiety, nausea and 8 kg weight loss. OGD shows a diffusely thickened, non-distensible stomach with no discrete mass or ulcer. Biopsies show cells with mucin pushing the nucleus to the edge, infiltrating the wall singly. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diffuse (signet ring cell) gastric adenocarcinoma infiltrates the wall without a discrete mass and has a worse prognosis than the intestinal type.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: mucin pushing the nucleus to the edge
steps.x: Signet ring cells infiltrating without a mass: the diffuse type (linitis plastica).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma.

elim: Shows a lymphoid infiltrate, not mucin-filled cells.
A submucosal mass of spindle cells.
Forms gland-like structures and a discrete mass, often after intestinal metaplasia.
Giant folds with foveolar hyperplasia, not malignant cells.

steps.x: **A. Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma.** Signet ring cells + no discrete mass = diffuse-type gastric cancer.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has had pernicious anaemia for 20 years, treated with hydroxocobalamin injections. For 3 months she has had epigastric pain, nausea and 5 kg weight loss that has not improved with omeprazole. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 80 bpm. Her B12 level is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia causes chronic atrophic gastritis and achlorhydria, predisposing to metaplasia and gastric adenocarcinoma; dyspepsia with weight loss and no PPI response needs urgent OGD.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Pernicious anaemia gives atrophic gastritis and achlorhydria, a set-up for gastric cancer; weight loss and PPI failure are red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastric adenocarcinoma.

elim: A diagnosis of exclusion; weight loss is a red flag.
Would respond to PPI and does not cause weight loss.
Her B12 is normal and it does not cause epigastric pain.
A neurological complication with no GI symptoms.

steps.x: **B. Gastric adenocarcinoma.** Pernicious anaemia + new dyspepsia + weight loss = gastric cancer.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the gastric antrum has 4 days of large-volume vomiting of food eaten the day before, without bile. He has epigastric fullness and a succussion splash. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: An antral gastric cancer can cause gastric outlet obstruction, with non-bilious vomiting, a succussion splash and hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; it needs urgent hospital management.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.

clues: vomiting of food eaten the day before
steps.x: An antral tumour blocking the pylorus: non-bilious vomiting of old food and a splash, with hypochloraemic alkalosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gastric outlet obstruction.

elim: Causes sudden pain and peritonism, not a succussion splash.
Causes nausea but not undigested food vomiting with a splash.
Causes distension and absolute constipation, vomiting late and faeculent.
He is not on opioids, and a splash with antral cancer suggests a mechanical block.

steps.x: **A. Gastric outlet obstruction.** Antral cancer + old-food vomiting + succussion splash = gastric outlet obstruction.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman had a Billroth I partial gastrectomy for an early antral adenocarcinoma 6 weeks ago. Within 20 minutes of eating, especially sweet foods, she gets palpitations, sweating, abdominal cramps, light-headedness and diarrhoea. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm at rest.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gastrectomy, such as Billroth I (partial gastrectomy with gastroduodenal anastomosis), can be complicated by early dumping: GI and vasomotor symptoms within 30 minutes of eating; late dumping is hypoglycaemia hours later.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, examination and tests.
Symptoms within 30 minutes of a meal after gastrectomy: rapid emptying into the small bowel.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Early dumping syndrome.

elim: Follows Billroth II with bilious vomiting, not after Billroth I.
Occurs within days with fever, pain and sepsis.
Reactive hypoglycaemia 1 to 3 hours after a meal.
Would cause weight loss and pain, not meal-timed autonomic symptoms.

steps.x: **C. Early dumping syndrome.** Post-gastrectomy symptoms within 30 minutes of eating = early dumping.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has 2 months of epigastric pain and 6 kg weight loss. A CT abdomen arranged by his GP for abdominal pain shows thickening of the gastric antral wall. There are no other abnormalities. His temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 78 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Endoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing gastric cancer; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is for staging afterwards.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.

clues: epigastric pain and 6 kg weight loss
thickening of the gastric antral wall
steps.x: You need tissue to make the diagnosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy.

elim: May show a filling defect but cannot provide tissue.
Tests for H. pylori, not cancer.
Stages the cancer once confirmed; it cannot give histology.
Used for occult metastases, not tissue diagnosis.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy.** Diagnose with OGD and biopsy; stage with CT.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a gastric adenocarcinoma in the body of the stomach confirmed on OGD biopsy. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases or enlarged nodes. The MDT needs to know how deeply the tumour invades the gastric wall and whether nearby nodes are involved before planning treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Gastric cancer is staged with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for distant spread, plus endoscopic ultrasound for local invasion and nodes.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.

clues: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases
how deeply the tumour invades the gastric wall
steps.x: CT has staged distant disease; local depth (T stage) and nearby nodes need EUS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endoscopic ultrasound.

elim: Shows lumen outline, not depth of invasion.
Brain metastases are rare and not routinely sought.
Delays treatment and does not assess local invasion better.
A tumour marker that does not stage.

steps.x: **B. Endoscopic ultrasound.** Distant spread = CT CAP; local invasion = EUS.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has 6 weeks of upper abdominal pain after meals. He has no dysphagia and no GI bleeding. His GP is deciding whether he meets the criteria for urgent referral for upper GI endoscopy on the suspected cancer pathway. Several further details are taken from the history.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most strongly indicate urgent endoscopy?
o: Coffee intake of 5 cups a day
Positive H. pylori serology in his brother
questions.e: Urgent (2-week wait) OGD is indicated for upper abdominal pain with weight loss, dysphagia or age over 55 with dyspepsia and weight loss; bloating and positional symptoms are not red flags.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Under 55, so age alone does not qualify; weight loss with upper abdominal pain does.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unintentional weight loss of 5 kg.

elim: A common, non-specific symptom.
A lifestyle trigger, not a red flag.
Not an indication for urgent endoscopy.
Suggests reflux, not cancer.

steps.x: **E. Unintentional weight loss of 5 kg.** Weight loss with upper abdominal symptoms = 2-week wait OGD.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has 3 months of dyspepsia not helped by lansoprazole, and fatigue and breathlessness on stairs. She has lost 4 kg. She takes no NSAIDs or anticoagulants. She has pale conjunctivae. Her GP sends blood tests before her urgent endoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?
questions.e: Gastric cancer commonly presents with dyspepsia not responding to PPI and anaemia, usually microcytic iron deficiency from chronic occult blood loss.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Chronic occult bleeding from a gastric tumour gives iron deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low haemoglobin with low MCV.

elim: Polycythaemia does not fit pallor and fatigue.
Macrocytic anaemia suggests B12 or folate deficiency.
Does not explain pallor.
Does not explain pallor and breathlessness.

steps.x: **C. Low haemoglobin with low MCV.** GI cancer anaemia = microcytic, iron deficient.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with known gastric adenocarcinoma has sudden severe epigastric pain that started 3 hours ago and is now across his whole abdomen. He lies still. His abdomen is rigid with guarding. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Gastric perforation from a tumour causes peritonitis with pneumoperitoneum; an erect chest X-ray shows air under the diaphragm (CT if unclear); endoscopy and barium are contraindicated.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what you need to know and which test answers it best.
Suspected perforation: look for air under the diaphragm quickly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Erect chest X-ray.

elim: Gas obscures views and it is not the first test for free air.
Barium in the peritoneum causes severe peritonitis.
Useful for pancreatitis, but free air must be sought first.
Insufflation could worsen a perforation.

steps.x: **C. Erect chest X-ray.** Suspected perforation: erect chest X-ray for free air.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman sees her GP with 6 weeks of dyspepsia and 4 kg unintentional weight loss. She has no dysphagia. Abdominal examination is normal. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Carbon-13 urea breath test and treat if positive
Full-dose PPI for 4 weeks and review
Refer on the 2-week wait pathway for upper GI endoscopy
questions.e: Under the 2-week wait suspected upper GI cancer pathway, anyone 55 or over with weight loss and dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain or reflux needs urgent OGD; test and treat is for those without red flags.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Over 55 with dyspepsia and weight loss: suspected upper GI cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Refer on the 2-week wait pathway for upper GI endoscopy.

elim: Test and treat is for dyspepsia without red flags.
Delays a cancer diagnosis in a patient with red flags.
Not urgent enough for suspected cancer.
Endoscopy with biopsy is the first test.

steps.x: **D. Refer on the 2-week wait pathway for upper GI endoscopy.** 55 or over + weight loss + dyspepsia = 2-week wait OGD.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a 2 cm adenocarcinoma of the distal gastric antrum. Endoscopic ultrasound shows it is confined to the submucosa, and CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no nodal or distant spread. He is fit for surgery. The surgeon plans to remove the distal stomach and join the remnant directly to the duodenum.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate procedure?
questions.e: Early gastric cancer is treated by surgical resection; a Billroth I partial gastrectomy joins the gastric remnant to the duodenum.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.

clues: join the remnant directly to the duodenum
steps.x: Early distal disease is cured by resection; a gastroduodenal anastomosis defines Billroth I.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Billroth I partial gastrectomy.

elim: Palliative for obstruction, not curative.
For oesophageal cancer.
An anti-reflux operation.
For pancreatic head cancer.

steps.x: **A. Billroth I partial gastrectomy.** Early gastric cancer = gastrectomy; gastroduodenal anastomosis = Billroth I.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has a gastric adenocarcinoma invading through the muscularis propria with two enlarged perigastric nodes on endoscopic ultrasound. CT shows no distant metastases. She is fit, with a performance status of 0. The MDT recommends chemotherapy before and after gastrectomy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate chemotherapy regimen?
questions.e: Locally advanced gastric cancer is treated with perioperative chemotherapy, typically FLOT (5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel), around gastrectomy.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Locally advanced, resectable gastric cancer: perioperative chemotherapy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: FLOT.

elim: The CROSS regimen for oesophageal cancer.
Mainly for pancreatic cancer.
Single-agent taxane is not standard perioperative therapy.
Used for non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

steps.x: **B. FLOT.** Locally advanced gastric cancer = perioperative FLOT.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with a known, untreated gastric adenocarcinoma vomits a large amount of fresh blood and has black stools. He is pale and clammy. His temperature is 36.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 86/54 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Haemoglobin is 68 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Bleeding from gastric cancer needs urgent hospital management: resuscitation with IV access, fluids and blood, then urgent endoscopy for haemostasis.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.

clues: vomits a large amount of fresh blood
steps.x: Shocked upper GI bleed from the tumour: ABCDE, fluids/blood, then endoscopy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Resuscitate and arrange urgent endoscopy.

elim: He is shocked; this needs emergency care.
Does not deal with active haemorrhage now.
Ignores life-threatening bleeding.
Does not stop an acute bleed.

steps.x: **E. Resuscitate and arrange urgent endoscopy.** Bleeding gastric cancer: resuscitate, then urgent endoscopy.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman has an adenocarcinoma of the gastric cardia with liver metastases. She now can only swallow liquids and is losing weight. She wants to be able to eat soft food again. Her performance status is 3. Her temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of her dysphagia?
questions.e: Obstructive symptoms of advanced gastric cancer are controlled with endoscopic stenting; resection is not appropriate with metastases.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Metastatic, frail, obstructing tumour: palliate the obstruction quickly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endoscopic stenting.

elim: An anti-reflux operation.
Used for achalasia; risky and short-lived in a tumour.
Not appropriate with liver metastases and poor fitness.
Does not restore swallowing and carries line risks.

steps.x: **A. Endoscopic stenting.** Malignant obstruction in advanced disease = endoscopic stent.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has signet ring cell gastric adenocarcinoma. CT shows bilateral ovarian masses and peritoneal deposits. She is otherwise fit, with performance status 1, and wants treatment that may help her live longer. Her temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 78 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Metastatic gastric cancer (here Krukenberg tumours and peritoneal deposits) is treated with palliative chemotherapy in fit patients; perioperative FLOT and gastrectomy are for non-metastatic disease.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Krukenberg and peritoneal spread mean metastatic disease: not curable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palliative chemotherapy.

elim: Does not treat the primary or peritoneal disease.
Only for obstructive symptoms, which she does not have.
For locally advanced disease without metastases.
Curative surgery is not appropriate with metastatic disease.

steps.x: **C. Palliative chemotherapy.** Metastatic gastric cancer, fit = palliative chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with gastric adenocarcinoma awaiting surgery has 2 hours of sudden severe abdominal pain. His abdomen is rigid. An erect chest X-ray (see item resources) is taken. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.

visual.title: Erect chest X-ray
visual.caption: Free air under both hemidiaphragms: pneumoperitoneum.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral PPI and review in clinic
Resuscitate, IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review
questions.e: Gastric perforation causes peritonitis and pneumoperitoneum; manage with resuscitation, nil by mouth, IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review.

steps.x: It asks what to do: decide where the patient is on the pathway and what comes next.
Air under the diaphragm in a peritonitic patient: perforated tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Resuscitate, IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review.

elim: He is septic with peritonitis.
Treats obstruction, not perforation.
Does not address a surgical emergency.
Insufflation worsens a perforation.

steps.x: **D. Resuscitate, IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review.** Free air + peritonitis = resuscitate and call the surgeons.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with long-standing untreated H. pylori infection has an intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma. Biopsies of the surrounding mucosa show loss of glands and areas where the lining contains goblet cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely sequence of changes leading to this cancer?
o: Chronic inflammation, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, cancer
Foveolar hyperplasia, achlorhydria, protein loss, cancer
questions.e: H. pylori causes chronic inflammation, then atrophic gastritis, then intestinal metaplasia, the precursor to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Goblet cells in gastric mucosa are intestinal metaplasia after atrophy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic inflammation, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, cancer.

elim: Ulceration and perforation are not steps toward cancer.
Describes Menetrier's disease.
Not what happens in the stomach.
Describes a GIST.

steps.x: **B. Chronic inflammation, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, cancer.** H. pylori: inflammation, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, cancer.

questions.stem: Two patients have gastric adenocarcinoma. The first has an ulcerated mass forming glands. The second has signet ring cells spreading through a thickened stomach wall with no discrete mass. The second patient is told her outlook is worse.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for the worse prognosis of the second tumour?
o: It infiltrates the wall without forming a discrete mass
It is a squamous cell carcinoma
It is caused by Epstein–Barr virus
It is the most common subtype
questions.e: Adenocarcinoma is the commonest subtype; the diffuse (signet ring cell) type infiltrates without forming a discrete mass, so it presents late and has a worse prognosis than the intestinal type.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Diffuse spread through the wall is detected late and is hard to resect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It infiltrates the wall without forming a discrete mass.

elim: Describes a carcinoid tumour.
Gastric cancer is mainly adenocarcinoma.
Not the reason diffuse-type is worse.
The intestinal type is more common; commonness does not worsen prognosis.

steps.x: **B. It infiltrates the wall without forming a discrete mass.** Diffuse type = infiltrative, no mass, worse prognosis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with signet ring cell gastric adenocarcinoma has bilateral ovarian masses. The ovaries are diffusely infiltrated by the same cells, and her peritoneal fluid contains tumour cells. A student asks how the cancer reached her ovaries.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of spread to the ovaries?
o: Haematogenous spread via the portal vein
Lymphatic spread via the thoracic duct
Transcoelomic spread across the peritoneal cavity
questions.e: Krukenberg tumours arise from spread of signet ring cells to the ovaries, mainly transcoelomic (also lymphatic or haematogenous); the thoracic duct route explains Virchow's node.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Tumour cells in peritoneal fluid seed the ovaries: transcoelomic spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Transcoelomic spread across the peritoneal cavity.

elim: The diaphragm is not between the stomach and the ovaries.
Portal spread goes to the liver.
Explains Virchow's node.
Not a route of metastasis to the ovaries.

steps.x: **E. Transcoelomic spread across the peritoneal cavity.** Krukenberg = transcoelomic spread; Virchow = thoracic duct.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man had a partial gastrectomy for gastric cancer. Shortly after meals he gets cramps, diarrhoea, palpitations and faintness. His symptoms are worst after sugary drinks and better when he eats small, dry meals and lies down after eating.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
o: Bacterial overgrowth in a blind loop
Bile reflux into the gastric remnant
Hyperosmolar food entering the small bowel and drawing in fluid
Reactive hypoglycaemia 2 hours after a meal
questions.e: Early dumping after gastrectomy is caused by rapid emptying of hyperosmolar contents into the small bowel, drawing fluid into the lumen, with distension and vasomotor symptoms.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the clinical finding to the underlying process.
Without the pylorus, sugary food rushes into the small bowel and pulls fluid in.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hyperosmolar food entering the small bowel and drawing in fluid.

elim: Causes chronic diarrhoea and B12 deficiency, not meal-timed faintness.
Causes bilious vomiting and pain.
That is late dumping.
Gives vomiting and weight loss.

steps.x: **C. Hyperosmolar food entering the small bowel and drawing in fluid.** Early dumping = hyperosmolar fluid shift into the bowel.
